sections.h2: What should an Illinois home seller know about the state before looking at a city or county guide?
sections.html:
A house sale in Illinois sits under statewide statutes, yet 102 county offices carry them out. The Code of Civil Procedure, the Property Tax Code and the Probate Act apply from the Wisconsin line to the Ohio River. Which recorder takes your deed, which collector sends your tax bill and which circuit clerk holds your eviction or foreclosure file depends on the county.

The sections below cover the statewide rules first. Local guides then add the county detail.

sections.h2: How is Illinois organized into counties and regions?
sections.html:
The basic unit of government is the county, and Illinois has 102 of them. Eighty-five of those counties are split further into townships and precincts, and cities, villages and incorporated towns run their own municipal governments, some with home rule powers, according to the state's Wikipedia entry on its government. Springfield is the capital and Chicago is the largest city. Cook is the largest county.

Geographers describe three broad divisions. Northern Illinois is dominated by Chicagoland, the city and its suburbs plus the exurban ring around them, and the metro area holds about 75% of the state's residents. Central Illinois is historically prairie and now mostly agricultural, with small towns and medium-sized cities. Southern Illinois reaches down to the confluence of the Ohio and Mississippi Rivers near Cairo. Each region has its own mix of buyers and housing.

sections.h2: How does Illinois property tax work for a seller?
sections.html:
Only local governments levy property tax in Illinois, roughly 6,000 units in all, and school districts take the largest share. The Illinois Department of Revenue explains that a tax year is the year of assessment, valued as of January 1, while the bills are paid the following year. A bill built on a 2023 assessment, for example, is paid in 2024. That lag is why the tax proration at closing deserves attention.

  • Every county except Cook has a required assessment level of 33 1/3 percent of the property's fair market value, with farmland and farm buildings treated separately.
  • Cook County classifies property, and its residential class carries a required level of 10 percent.
  • The General Homestead Exemption lowers the equalized assessed value for a homeowner who lives in the house. The exempt amount cannot exceed $6,000 in most counties, $8,000 in counties contiguous to Cook, and $10,000 in Cook County.

Disputes over value go to the county board of review, with a Cook County owner starting at the assessor. The assessment change notice lists the filing deadlines, and a bill in hand usually means the window has closed. Ask the treasurer or collector for the current bill before signing a contract.

sections.h2: What shapes the housing market outside Chicago?
sections.html:
Illinois entered the Union on December 3, 1818, as the 21st state, and its economy grew from river and prairie trade into a mix that few states match. Chicago serves as a global city for the Midwest, the north and center hold major industrial and farm hubs, and the south has coal, timber and petroleum. The Port of Chicago reaches the Atlantic through the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence Seaway, and the state's central location makes it a freight crossroads.

A farm county, a suburban collar county and a river town each run their own county offices, so ask the local recorder and treasurer about filing methods before a closing date is set.

sections.h2: What limits and relief programs affect Illinois tax bills?
sections.html: The Property Tax Extension Limitation Law restricts growth in a taxing district's property tax revenue to 5 percent or the annual change in the Consumer Price Index, whichever is less, unless voters approve a higher rate. It first covered Lake, DuPage, Kane, McHenry and Will counties, reached Cook County in 1995, and spread to other counties by referendum, with 33 counties on board in the 2023 revision of the state overview. Seniors with household income of $65,000 or less can defer all or part of the tax on a home through the Senior Citizens Real Estate Tax Deferral Program, and the deferred tax plus interest generally comes due when the owner sells or dies. That detail matters in an estate sale, where the deferred balance shows up at closing. Homeowners may also claim a credit of up to 5 percent on their state income tax for property tax paid on a primary residence.

sections.h2: What transfer tax applies when an Illinois deed is recorded?
sections.html: The state transfer tax statute, 35 ILCS 200/31-15, says the county recorder or registrar of titles collects the tax and sells revenue stamps at 50¢ for each $500 of value or fraction of $500. The section also moves counties from paper stamps to electronic ones after 2025. Ask the recorder's office for your property for the recording fee, the required forms and any local transfer charges on top of the state rate. The city and county guides here cover the larger offices.

sections.h2: Which state rules matter most for a distressed Illinois sale?
sections.html:
Three topics shape most urgent sales, and each has its own guide.

  • Foreclosure. Illinois forecloses through the courts. A mortgagor may reinstate within 90 days after service, and residential redemption ends on the later of 7 months after service or 3 months after judgment. Cook County runs a free mortgage foreclosure mediation program through its Chancery Division.
  • Eviction. A rent demand gives at least 5 days, a lease default gets a 10 day notice, and tenancies with no default end on 7, 30 or 60 days of notice depending on the term. Only a court order ends the tenancy by force.
  • Probate. Under 755 ILCS 5/25-1, a small estate affidavit works only when no letters of office are outstanding and the personal estate stays within $150,000, registered motor vehicles aside. It addresses personal property, so ask a probate attorney how a house in the estate gets transferred.

A homeowner who stops paying property tax risks a lien sale. The state's overview gives residential property of six units or fewer two and one-half years from the sale date to redeem, with penalties and costs added.

sections.h2: Where should an Illinois seller start with the local guides?
sections.html:
Pick the county first. Its recorder, assessor, treasurer and circuit clerk handle most of the paper. A city guide adds permit, rental and neighborhood detail, and the statewide topic guides cover foreclosure, eviction, probate and tax rules that hold in every county. Before relying on a figure, confirm it with the office that issues the bill or form.

Inherited houses, payment trouble and rentals with tenants are the usual reasons owners sell fast. The recording, tax and court steps above still apply however the sale is structured.

faqs.q: How many counties does Illinois have?
faqs.a: Illinois has 102 counties. Eighty-five of them are divided into townships and precincts, and municipal governments such as cities, villages and incorporated towns operate alongside them. Cook County is the largest by population.

faqs.q: When did Illinois become a state, and what is its capital?
faqs.a: Illinois was admitted to the Union on December 3, 1818, as the 21st state, and Springfield is the capital. Chicago is the largest city, and the Chicago metro area holds about three quarters of the population.

faqs.q: What is the Illinois real estate transfer tax rate?
faqs.a: The state rate in section 31-15 is 50¢ for each $500 of value or fraction of $500, collected by the county recorder or registrar of titles. Ask the recorder's office for the property for any local charges beyond the state rate.

faqs.q: Does the small estate affidavit cover a house?
faqs.a: No. The affidavit in 755 ILCS 5/25-1 addresses personal property up to $150,000, registered vehicles aside. For a house, speak with a probate attorney.

faqs.q: Is there free foreclosure help in Illinois?
faqs.a: Yes in Cook County, where the Chancery Division mediation program gives homeowners who received a summons free housing counseling and legal assistance. Elsewhere, ask the circuit clerk in your county whether a similar program exists.
